findings.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:200 — user.errors.to_hash` relies on ActiveModel::Errors JSON-serializing symbol keys as strings for the JS's `result.errors.email` lookup to work; this is correct for standard Rails `to_json` behavior but is an implicit contract (no test asserts `errors` is keyed by `"email"` as a string in the JSON body), so a Rails/ActiveModel upgrade or custom `as_json` override elsewhere could silently change key casing/type and break the new client logic with no test catching it.

db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — action_type` is `null: false` at the DB level but has no DB-level default; the only default comes from `BlockedEmail#set_defaults` (a `before_validation` callback in app/models/blocked_email.rb:3-4,23-25), so any insert path that bypasses AR validations/callbacks (raw SQL, `insert_all`, `update_column`, console `BlockedEmail.new(email: x).save(validate: false)`, future seed/import migrations) will hit a NOT NULL constraint violation instead of getting a sane default.

db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:6 — action_type` is a raw integer enum column with no DB-level CHECK constraint tying it to `BlockedEmail.actions` (block/do_nothing); any out-of-range value written outside the app layer (raw SQL, manual DB edits) will silently pass the schema and only fail later, if at all, in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` logic.

app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — values: user.attributes.slice("name","username","email")` echoes attacker-supplied signup fields back into the JSON response for no functional need (only `email` is consumed client-side); unnecessary reflection of user input expands the response surface for future unsanitized consumption.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:200 — user.errors.to_hash` relies on ActiveModel::Errors JSON-serializing symbol keys as strings for the JS's `result.errors.email` lookup to work; this is correct for standard Rails `to_json` behavior but is an implicit contract (no test asserts `errors` is keyed by `"email"` as a string in the JSON body), so a Rails/ActiveModel upgrade or custom `as_json` override elsewhere could silently change key casing/type and break the new client logic with no test catching it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `errors: user.errors.to_hash` to the JSON response in `UsersController#create` and the client now checks `result.errors && result.errors.email` before pushing `result.values.email` into `rejectedEmails`. This does implicitly rely on Rails JSON encoding producing a JS object with an `"email"` property (i.e., stringified keys) from the `to_hash` output. While this works under typical Rails behavior, the diff adds no test asserting the response `errors` structure/keys used by the new client logic, so a change in serialization/as_json could break the feature without coverage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:5 — action_type` is `null: false` at the DB level but has no DB-level default; the only default comes from `BlockedEmail#set_defaults` (a `before_validation` callback in app/models/blocked_email.rb:3-4,23-25), so any insert path that bypasses AR validations/callbacks (raw SQL, `insert_all`, `update_column`, console `BlockedEmail.new(email: x).save(validate: false)`, future seed/import migrations) will hit a NOT NULL constraint violation instead of getting a sane default.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `blocked_emails.action_type` is `null: false` in the migration (no DB default), while the only defaulting happens in `BlockedEmail#set_defaults` via `before_validation` (`self.action_type ||= BlockedEmail.actions[:block]`). That means inserts that skip validations/callbacks (e.g., `save(validate: false)` or bulk/SQL insert paths) can hit a NOT NULL violation instead of receiving the intended default. This is a concrete, diff-grounded robustness/consistency issue, though normal AR `create`/`save` flows will work.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb:6 — action_type` is a raw integer enum column with no DB-level CHECK constraint tying it to `BlockedEmail.actions` (block/do_nothing); any out-of-range value written outside the app layer (raw SQL, manual DB edits) will silently pass the schema and only fail later, if at all, in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` logic.

adjudication.rationale: The migration creates `blocked_emails.action_type` as a plain `integer` with `null: false` but no DB-level constraint limiting values to the defined enum (`BlockedEmail.actions` => `:block`, `:do_nothing`). The model also doesn’t validate inclusion of `action_type` in that enum. This isn’t a guaranteed runtime defect in normal app flows (the app sets a default and compares against `actions[:block]`), but it is a concrete robustness/data-integrity gap: out-of-range values inserted outside the app layer would be accepted by the schema and could lead to unexpected behavior in `BlockedEmail.should_block?`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/controllers/users_controller.rb:198 — values: user.attributes.slice("name","username","email")` echoes attacker-supplied signup fields back into the JSON response for no functional need (only `email` is consumed client-side); unnecessary reflection of user input expands the response surface for future unsanitized consumption.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `UsersController#create` to include `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` in the JSON failure response. On the client side, the only new consumption shown is `result.values.email` in `create_account_controller.js` when pushing into `rejectedEmails`; there is no diff-shown use of `name` or `username`. Echoing extra attacker-supplied fields back is unnecessary per the shown client logic and does widen the response surface for any future (potentially unsafe) usage, but the diff alone doesn’t prove an exploitable defect today.
